verses.text: But God remembered Noah and all the animals and livestock that were with him in the ark. And God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside.
The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the heavens were closed, and the rain from the sky was restrained.
The waters receded steadily from the earth, and after 150 days the waters had gone down.
On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
And the waters continued to recede until the tenth month, and on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains became visible.
After forty days Noah opened the window he had made in the ark
and sent out a raven. It kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth.
Then Noah sent out a dove to see if the waters had receded from the surface of the ground.

But the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him in the ark, because the waters were still covering the surface of all the earth. So he reached out his hand and brought her back inside the ark.
Noah waited seven more days and again sent out the dove from the ark.
And behold, the dove returned to him in the evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak. So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth.
And Noah waited seven more days and sent out the dove again, but this time she did not return to him.

In Noah's six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters had dried up from the earth. So Noah removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry.
By the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth was fully dry.
Then God said to Noah,
"Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives.
Bring out all the living creatures that are with you—birds, livestock, and everything that crawls upon the ground—so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it."
So Noah came out, along with his sons and his wife and his sons' wives.
Every living creature, every creeping thing, and every bird—everything that moves upon the earth—came out of the ark, kind by kind.
Then Noah built an altar to the LORD. And taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar.

When the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, He said in His heart, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man, even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth. And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done.
As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall never cease."

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Narrative of beginnings (Genesis 1-11): creation, the first family, the flood and the nations, with genealogies
context.audience: Israel, God’s covenant people, learning who their God is, where the world came from and what went wrong with it
context.setting: “But God remembered Noah” (v.1). He sends a wind over the earth, the springs of the deep and the floodgates of heaven are closed, and the waters go down (vv.1-3). On the seventeenth day of the seventh month the ark comes to rest “on the mountains of Ararat” (v.4). Noah sends out a raven, then a dove, which finds nowhere to rest; seven days later the dove comes back with “a freshly plucked olive leaf” (vv.6-11), and the next time it does not return (v.12). The earth is dry by the twenty-seventh day of the second month, a little over a year after the flood began (v.14). God says, “Come out of the ark” (v.16). Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings, and the LORD smells “the pleasing aroma” (vv.20-21). He promises never again to curse the ground or strike down every living thing: “As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall never cease” (v.22).
context.custom: Sailors in the ancient world carried birds to find land. In the Gilgamesh epic Utnapishtim sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven; when the gods smell his sacrifice they ‘gathered like flies.’ Genesis tells it differently: one God, who remembers and makes a promise. Ararat is the region later called Urartu, around Lake Van in eastern Turkey and Armenia; the peak now named Mount Ararat took the name later.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 9 tells of God’s covenant with Noah and every living creature, with the rainbow as its sign.
context.timelineBible: “God remembered” marks turning points of rescue in Genesis and Exodus: He remembered Abraham and saved Lot (19:29), remembered Rachel (30:22), and remembered His covenant with Israel in Egypt (Exodus 2:24). The dove has become a sign of peace; at Jesus’ baptism the Spirit descended “like a dove” (Matthew 3:16). Paul calls Christ’s self-giving “a fragrant sacrificial offering to God” (Ephesians 5:2).

translation.meaning: To remember. With God it means more than recalling: He acts on what He has promised.
Wind, breath, spirit. The same word as ‘the Spirit of God’ over the waters in 1:2: a new beginning like the first.
Soothing, restful, pleasing: another play on Noah’s name (noach, rest). The phrase ‘a pleasing aroma’ becomes a regular term for sacrifices in the law.

gospelParallels.note: The Spirit of God descending like a dove.
Christ gave Himself up for us as a fragrant offering.
He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons.

otBackground.note: God heard their groaning and remembered His covenant.
A burnt offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
My covenant with the day and the night.

overview.summary: God remembers Noah, the waters go down, the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat, the dove brings back an olive leaf, and Noah leaves the ark and offers sacrifice; God promises that seedtime and harvest will never cease.

history.t: The kingdom around Lake Van, the Bible’s Ararat.
Ancient sailors used birds to look for land.

customs.t: The whole animal given to God on the altar.
A sign that trees were growing again.

archaeology.t: Assyrian records and ruins around Lake Van show the kingdom of Urartu (9th-6th century BC).
Utnapishtim sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven.

overview.discussion: “As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest… shall never cease” (v.22). Where do I see God’s faithfulness in the ordinary rhythm of seasons and days?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters (1-25 in the app so far). Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham and his family.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

Sent out to find dry land
